manifold

MAN-uh-fohld -- stress on the first syllable, MAN. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Manifold is numerous and various.

The principal's manifold duties ranged from approving budgets to judging the fourth-grade science fair.

Example

In one afternoon, the park ranger handles manifold tasks: repairing a trail sign, rescuing a lost hiker, testing the lake water, filing a wildfire report, and teaching a class of scouts to read a compass.

The tasks are not just numerous but strikingly varied, spanning many different kinds of work. Manifold describes things that are many and diverse at the same time.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

diverse: Diverse means made up of many different kinds -- a diverse cast comes from many backgrounds. Manifold covers more ground: manifold duties are not only varied in kind but also large in number. A small committee of three very different people is diverse; it is too few to be manifold.

varied: Varied means showing differences from one item to the next -- a varied menu offers several distinct dishes. Manifold is stronger and more formal: manifold responsibilities are both many and varied, sheer quantity and wide range at once. A list can be varied with only four entries; manifold implies far more.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

identical: exactly alike

few: small in number

Where it sits · how many different kinds it spans — numerous → manifold → multifarious

numerous vs. manifold: Numerous counts heads and nothing more, so it is weaker than manifold -- numerous complaints are simply many, while manifold complaints are many and of many different kinds.

multifarious vs. manifold: Multifarious out-varies even manifold: manifold duties are numerous and varied, while multifarious ones sprawl across so many unrelated categories that no single person could sort them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mani

Root — mani: many (from Old English manig, 'many')

Suffix — -fold

Suffix — -fold: times, ways (Old English -feald)

Put it together

Put it together: Mani ('many' — from Old English manig) + -fold ('times, ways,' Old English -feald): literally 'many ways.' Things that are manifold do not just come in large numbers; they come in many different kinds, folded together from every direction.

Use the root in a new word: tenfold

Use the root in a new word: tenfold: By harvest time, the seed money the farmers had pooled together came back tenfold.

Root Check

Word Choice

Manifold is a formal, slightly literary adjective that sits before plural nouns: manifold reasons, manifold challenges, manifold blessings. Choose it when you mean many and varied -- if the items are all of one kind, plain 'many' is the honest word.
